transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Cosmos CTO), Sofia Martinez (Lead ML), Ravi Patel (Infra), Lena Wu (Product)

Summary (auto): medium confidence. Technical deep dive on KV-cache eviction and paging for long-context chat workloads.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, from Redwood we have Liam and Priya as well. Quick agenda — dig into the eviction behavior you saw, validate telemetry, and propose a bench plan.
[00:18] Daniel Park: Hi all, thanks. We've been seeing intermittent failures with long sessions; basically, after a few hours of simulated user traffic some requests get longer tail latency and occasionally truncated outputs.
[00:32] Sofia Martinez: Yeah to add — we reuse prefixes across threads (customer profile + product context) and after reuse across many users we start hitting what looks like kv eviction; tokens aren't found in cache and it falls back to full compute and latency spikes.
[00:50] Liam O'Connor: Got it. Can you remind us of your infra shape — are you on Redwood hosted or Dedicated or private?
[00:58] Ravi Patel: We're on Dedicated reserve right now but planning a VPC private pilot for PHI workflows later this quarter. All nodes are A100-ish, 80GB. We run mixed precision 4-bit quantized model (we call it q4f) in the stack.
[01:14] Priya Rao: Interesting — quantization + large batch windows can change KV memory pressure characteristics. The q4 path has slightly different KV cache per-key size, that might explain earlier eviction thresholds.
[01:28] Sofia Martinez: We thought quantization would reduce memory but we still see eviction sooner than expected even with smaller model weights.
[01:35] Maya Chen: Two things to check: (1) per-request prefix reuse patterns — are you concatenating many user-specific prefixes into a single session or creating many sessions that share prefixes? (2) KV paging settings — are you using our paging-to-SSD mode and what's your page-size?
[01:52] Daniel Park: We're mostly reusing the same prefix across sessions, but we also have a few very long system messages that are prepended. Paging is enabled but default thresholds — we didn't tune page-size.
[02:06] Liam O'Connor: Ok. When you say eviction, are you observing explicit "evict" logs or just misses and increased loads?
[02:14] Sofia Martinez: We see evict logs in the agent metrics. The timeline: after ~10k requests the cache miss rate jumps and CPU on the host jumps too.
[02:24] Maya Chen: That aligns with high churn in KV keys due to prefix reuse and long system messages. The runtime maintains a working set limited by configured kv cache memory and will evict least-recently-used keys; but if a few very long prefixes are touched across many sessions, they can push out more frequently used recent keys.
[02:43] Ravi Patel: Are there knob recommendations for page-size or eviction grace we can tune without impacting latency?
[02:50] Liam O'Connor: Yes — two levers: (A) increase in-memory KV capacity (memory budget) to avoid paging for the critical working set; (B) adjust eviction hysteresis and LRU window; (C) use prefix compaction — merge static shared prefixes into a single cached key rather than repeating; and (D) tune batching/streaming so the effective concurrency doesn't blow the working set.
[03:14] Sofia Martinez: Prefix compaction — can you explain? We have the same user profile inserted multiple times across different turns.
[03:22] Priya Rao: Sure — instead of storing repeated tokens for each session, we create a canonical prefix key for identical content and reference it from session state. That reduces duplicated cache entries and reduces pressure.
[03:34] Daniel Park: Would that require changes to our prompt assembly flow?
[03:37] Liam O'Connor: Minimal — just a normalization step on the client side that fingerprint prefixes and then pass a prefix-id to the runtime; Redwood's runtime will treat that as a shared key. We can share a snippet.
[03:50] Maya Chen: I'll add the snippet to the artifacts — we have an example in the KV-cache whitepaper. Link in chat.
[03:56] Lena Wu: Paging to SSD — is that safe for latency-sensitive flows?
[04:01] Priya Rao: It's a tradeoff. Paging reduces memory footprint but adds IO latency when a page is loaded back. For conversational flows with strict latency SLAs, we recommend keeping the hot working set in memory and using paging as a safety net. If you must use SSD paging, use large sequential reads and prefer NVMe with sustained IOPS.
[04:22] Ravi Patel: Our spikes correlate with multiple concurrent sessions hitting different prefixes. Any advice on batching settings?
[04:29] Liam O'Connor: Keep batch sizes small for latency critical requests—use batching only where tail-latency isn't critical. Also autoscale workers to keep concurrency per worker bounded; high concurrency increases total active KV entries.
[04:42] Sofia Martinez: You earlier mentioned quantization differences. Could q4 be inflating kv size vs q8?
[04:49] Priya Rao: Yes, the internal representation changes. Some q4 kernels store keys differently and overhead per KV entry can be higher for certain implementations. We have profiling data — we'll include it.
[05:00] Maya Chen: Another possible cause is prefix fragmentation from minor tokenization differences causing multiple near-identical keys. Are you normalizing tokenization across clients?
[05:10] Sofia Martinez: We're not; different clients use slightly different encoders in older browsers. Oof.
[05:15] Daniel Park: That's probably part of it. We'll work on normalizing client-side tokenization.
[05:20] Liam O'Connor: Good. On the observability side, increase KV cache telemetry (per-key hit counts, key-age histograms) and correlate with latency spikes. We also suggest a microbenchmark for eviction stress tests — script will produce repeatable key churn.
[05:36] Lena Wu: Can Redwood run that benchmark with us or do we run it?
[05:40] Liam O'Connor: We can run jointly; we'll produce a runbook. We'll need a representative sample of prefixes and a traffic profile.
[05:48] Maya Chen: Ok, next let's talk about the paging configuration you have. Can you paste current runtime config?
[05:54] Ravi Patel: Sure — config: kv_memory_budget: 110GB, paging: enabled, page_size: 256MB, eviction_hysteresis: default.
[06:05] Priya Rao: That budget seems small for the total working set you're describing on A100 80GB nodes — remember other runtime allocations also consume memory. We typically recommend starting with 25-40% of node RAM reserved for KV cache depending on batch sizes.
[06:20] Sofia Martinez: We're at 110GB across cluster? It's per-worker config; might need to re-evaluate.
[06:26] Liam O'Connor: Also check JVM or other process limits that can cause earlier pressure; or if other processes like monitoring agents are ballooning memory.
[06:36] Daniel Park: For our VPC/on-prem concerns, we need to ensure that the paging path doesn't leak data — encrypted at rest? KMS?
[06:44] Maya Chen: Yes — paging objects are encrypted at rest and we integrate with KMS/HSM for key management. In Private deploy we can support customer-managed keys and HSM. We'll include security docs.
[06:55] Lena Wu: SOC 2? Audit logs?
[06:58] Maya Chen: Redwood has SOC 2 and audit trail support; we'll attach the compliance pack.
[07:04] Sofia Martinez: Back to the eviction: are there thresholds to detect that kv eviction will soon start? Some early warning metric?
[07:12] Priya Rao: Hit-rate delta and tail latency correlate well; also track free KV entries and page fault rate. We'll provide a dashboard query.
[07:22] Liam O'Connor: For immediate mitigation, three options: bump kv budget, use prefix compaction, or reduce concurrency/adjust batching. For longer term, run the benchmark and tune the page_size and eviction_hysteresis.
[07:36] Daniel Park: About page_size — we currently use 256MB; any guidance?
[07:40] Priya Rao: It depends on workload. Larger page sizes reduce metadata overhead and aim for larger sequential reads, but if your working set has many small keys, it can increase unnecessary IO. We typically test 64MB, 128MB, 256MB and measure IO latency under realistic concurrency.
[07:58] Sofia Martinez: Does revised quantization pipeline (q8_0) change this behavior?
[08:03] Liam O'Connor: Possibly — q8 tends to be more memory efficient for KV in our internal tests. We'll share numbers for similar model families.
[08:12] Maya Chen: Quick note — prefix reuse and caching also interacts with our rollouts. If you pin different model variants for subset of traffic, KV keys are variant-specific. That can multiply effective working set. Are you doing canaries?
[08:26] Daniel Park: We did a small canary with a newer decoder — maybe that increased key variance. Good point.
[08:31] Priya Rao: So ensure keys include model-id normalization and consider shared canonical keys across compatible variants when possible.
[08:42] Ravi Patel: For the pilot, we want a reproducible test that simulates 10k concurrent chat sessions with 8k window and prefix reuse. Would Redwood be able to run such a test on Dedicated?
[08:52] Liam O'Connor: Yes — we'll coordinate capacity. We recommend staging with smaller scale first (1k) to iterate. The runbook will include ramp profiles and expected metrics.
[09:03] Maya Chen: We'll also include a test for prefix fragmentation — send near-identical prefixes with small tokenization differences and measure duplicate key explosion.
[09:12] Sofia Martinez: Perfect. A couple more quick questions: does eviction behavior differ for streaming vs non-streaming responses?
[09:19] Priya Rao: Streaming holds the KV during the request; long streaming requests can increase in-flight KV entries per session, so it can amplify pressure. Non-streaming can be slightly more memory-friendly per-request.
[09:33] Daniel Park: Any quick tuning for immediate triage? We could temporarily throttle concurrency.
[09:38] Liam O'Connor: Throttling is a fast mitigation; also increase kv_memory_budget by 10-20% on the worker pool and enable prefix compaction patch we will share.
[09:48] Maya Chen: Ok let's recap. Action items: Maya share docs and snippet; Liam create bench runbook; Sofia upload traces; Ravi check network/KMS; schedule run the week of 2027-01-25.
[10:02] Daniel Park: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:05] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with links.
[10:10] (meeting ends)

Transcript notes: transcription has a few mis-hearings (q4 -> q4f ambiguous, some model names omitted). References to docs are links in the chat but external content not included here.
